title: Predictive throttle orchestration and failover simulation framework
creator: Priya Nair
description: Problem: Dedicated and private control planes occasionally experience short, high-amplitude tenant surges (traffic spikes, noisy tenants after upgrades, or regional network flaps) that cause latency SLO violations and cascading tenant degradation. Current defenses are reactive (manual throttles, emergency capacity swaps) or coarse-grained (global admission limits, full-region failovers). We lack a codified, testable playbook for predictive throttles and multi-region staged failover that can be exercised against historical incidents and synthetic demand patterns.
goal: Design and deliver a 'Predictive Throttle Orchestrator' and an accompanying Failover Simulation Framework that let ops and platform engineers: 1) proactively apply tenant-scoped soft-throttles based on short-term demand forecasts and SLO risk, 2) automatically stage region failovers when predictive signals indicate imminent capacity collapse, and 3) validate policies via a replayable simulation harness using historical metrics and fuzzed traffic patterns.
acceptance_criteria: A1: A controller (orchestrator) can ingest short-term (5–60m) traffic forecasts and map them to per-tenant throttle actions (soft limit, reject, write-heavy vs read-heavy adjustments).

A2: Orchestrator exposes policy primitives: risk score threshold, throttle severity tiers, cooldown windows, escalation paths to region failover, and can be configured per-tenant and per-environment (dedicated vs private).

A3: Simulation framework can run recorded production metric streams (token throughput, latency percentiles, KV cache hit ratios) and inject synthetic failure events (region latency spikes, kernel OOMs).
A4: Policies validated in simulation preserve SLOs (p90 latency and availability) for high-priority tenants in at least 95% of replayed incidents compared to the baseline strategy.
A5: Integration tests and a canary in a staging dedicated cluster demonstrate automated throttle escalation and a safe staged region failover without manual intervention.
A6: Playbook and runbook documented with clear rollback steps, observability panels, and a post-incident checklist.
implementation_plan: 1) Design policy model: define inputs (short-term forecast, current token rate, in-flight KV cache size, latency p50/p95/p99, error rate), outputs (throttle_percent, route_remap, failover_signal), and cooldown/decay semantics.

2) Build a lightweight orchestrator service (k8s deployment) that subscribes to existing metrics stream (Prometheus/Pushgateway or Kafka), evaluates policies, and posts actions to the tenant admission controller API.
3) Add hooks to admission controller to accept soft throttle actions: graded token rejection, synthetic prioritization headers, and temporary traffic shaping windows.
4) Implement simulation harness: metric replayer, failure injector, and policy evaluator. Provide a CLI to run scenarios and a dashboard summarizing SLO outcomes for each policy variant.
5) Author default policy bundles for Dedicated and Private with conservative thresholds; ship as config maps and feature flags behind a rollout gate.
6) End-to-end integration tests in staging; run historical incident replays (last 18 months) to tune thresholds and escalation behavior.

7) Canary rollout: enable orchestrator for a small set of tenants in staging Dedicated, observe for 72h, then gradual ramp to 10% of production tenants with canary monitoring and rapid rollback automation.
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Design review and security review (2 weeks).
Phase 1: Dev + unit tests; local sim harness validated by SRE (2 weeks).
Phase 2: Staging integration, run historical replays, iterate policy (1 week).
Phase 3: Canary on non-critical tenants in a Dedicated cluster (72h) with manual guardrails.
Phase 4: Gradual ramp to 10% of tenants (7 days) with automated rollback on SLO regression alerts.
Phase 5: Full rollout to Dedicated, optional private customer opt-in.
metrics: Primary SLOs: p95 latency, availability (successful token responses) for pinned tenants.
Operational: number of throttle actions per hour, average throttle severity, false-positive throttle rate (actions where SLOs unchanged), time-to-escalation-to-failover.
Safety: successful automatic rollbacks triggered, incidents avoided (simulated) compared to baseline.
test_plan: Unit tests for policy evaluation logic (edge cases: missing metrics, conflicting actions).
Integration tests connecting orchestrator -> admission controller -> routing layer in staging.
Simulation runs: replay 6 high-severity incidents and 20 synthetic surge patterns, track SLO delta.
Chaos tests: run orchestrator while injecting partial control-plane partitions to validate graceful degradation and idempotence.
risks: Overthrottling: conservative policies must be chosen to avoid unnecessary customer impact.
False confidence from simulation if replayed datasets are not representative; need diverse fuzzing and edge-case injection.
Control-loop instability if forecasts are noisy — require smoothing and minimum hold windows.
Private deployments may restrict telemetry availability; need fallback modes that use local signals only.
open_questions: Q1: Which forecasting model do we adopt? Lightweight ARIMA-like smoothing or an ML model trained on tenant historical patterns?
Q2: How do we represent tenant priority and SLA metadata to the orchestrator (labels on tenant records or a separate policy store)?
Q3: For private deployments, what minimal telemetry must customers expose for safe operation, and can we provide a local-only orchestrator image?
Q4: What are SRE/Support escalation procedures if orchestrator repeatedly triggers for the same tenant?
